summary: Team AirmanPrep built two public web tools for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, each approaching the same problem from a different angle. SPHEREx Blink starts from the data: enter any RA/Dec and it plays a time-lapse of every real SPHEREx exposure covering that patch, fetched live from the NASA IRSA archive, with blink, difference and stack modes and a spectrum for any pixel. Barnard's Star visibly moves north in the real data. Planeta-X starts from the user: compare two epochs across four near-infrared bands, click an object that moved, draw its A to B vector and export the findings. Together they let anyone spot moving objects in SPHEREx-era infrared images without handling FITS files. Every SPHEREx Blink view is a shareable, embeddable URL, and a landing page explains why we built two tools and links both apps and both repositories.
details:
WHAT IT IS. Two public web tools, built by Team AirmanPrep for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Both help people spot moving objects in SPHEREx-era infrared images, from two different angles. The landing page at https://spherex.pdsx.org/ explains why we built two and links both apps and both repositories.

SPHEREX BLINK (by Luis). Starts from the data. A visitor types RA/Dec (decimal or sexagesimal) and a field of view; the app plays a time-lapse of every real SPHEREx exposure covering that patch, like a short video. It offers raw, epoch-difference, co-add and per-detector stack modes, so each comparison is like-for-like (same detector, same wavelength). Clicking a pixel assembles a spectrum from all covering exposures, with uncertainties and the quality flags read from each file's FITS header. The five challenge targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) are one-click presets. Every view is a URL, so it can be shared or embedded in an iframe. App: https://spherex-4e2z.onrender.com/ Source: https://github.com/Luis000923/SPHEREx

How it works: a Rust (axum) backend queries the IRSA SIA2 service for the epochs (with a TAP fallback) and reads only the needed byte ranges of each image from the public AWS Open Data mirror of the SPHEREx archive, decoding the multi-extension FITS files in its own bounds-checked reader (image, variance, flags, sky WCS and the per-pixel wavelength map). A science layer reprojects every cutout onto a common north-up grid. The React/TypeScript frontend draws frames on a WebGL2 canvas. IRSA is a shared public service, so the backend limits concurrency, retries with backoff and caches results; the five presets ship pre-cached.

What we measured on the real archive: Barnard's Star moves north at about 9 arcsec per year in our simple centroid tracking (catalogue value 10.4, our uncertainty about 2), and difference mode shows it as a bright and dark pair. Epsilon Indi B is an unresolved binary at SPHEREx's 6.15 arcsec per pixel, and WISE 0855 is too faint for single frames, so the app reports no detection for either instead of faking one.

PLANETA-X (by Charlie). Starts from the user. A guided epoch comparator: slide or blink between Epoch A and Epoch B across four near-infrared bands, click an object that changed position, and a second click in the other epoch draws its A to B trajectory vector. Findings are listed per region and can be exported to CSV or JSON. The interface is in Spanish and English, with a PHP API and a local demo mode that keeps findings in the browser. Its images are WISE cutouts from IRSA and simulated SPHEREx-style regions, not live SPHEREx exposures. App: https://app.planeta-x.earth Source: https://github.com/charlie-002-XD/Planeta-X

WHY TWO. SPHEREx Blink answers "what does the real archive show here?". Planeta-X answers "how would I mark and report a mover?". Neither replaces the other, and keeping them side by side lets judges compare both approaches.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT. Removes the barriers between SPHEREx data and the public: no FITS or archive knowledge needed, and results in seconds. Useful for classrooms, amateur astronomers and researchers previewing a position.

TOOLS. SPHEREx Blink: Rust (axum, tokio, reqwest, ndarray), TypeScript, React, Vite, WebGL2, uPlot, Aladin Lite, Docker. Planeta-X: React, Vite, TailwindCSS, Framer Motion, PHP, and Python scripts for the sample data. Landing page and presentation: PHP and static HTML on shared hosting.
